note: Stand-in summaries of the book (story-v4.json), written once from each scene's text by a model following the memory keeper's summary prompt (keeper/prompts.ts), for the offline recall measure. Invented story.

scenes.s1: By the end, Tamsin Orr and her brother Pim were back at the clock-house on Gilt Street, the great Guildhall clock was still stopped at seven minutes to midnight, and the crowd had begun to murmur the Orr name. Pim wanted to go up the tower and fix it at once, and Tamsin had forbidden it. On Lantern Night the whole of Callowmere crossed the Chain Bridge to hear the clock strike midnight, a clock that Tamsin's late father and his partner Edwin Leckie had built twelve years earlier. Tamsin, who kept the house's books and knew its money was thin, bought Pim chestnuts while he grumbled that Leckie, who had left at the end of autumn without a proper explanation, should have been there. Pim, who could read dials at a glance but had never learned to read words, was the first to notice that the clock had stopped. As the crowd turned to look at the Orrs, he said loudly that the clock was already theirs, which drew the attention of a man in a guild collar. Tamsin hauled him back across the bridge and home through the crowd, while he kept insisting he could have it running by morning.
scenes.s2: By the end, Tamsin sat alone in the counting room in the small hours holding a secret nobody else shared: a page in her father's last ledger, sewn shut with black silk, recorded a loan of four hundred and twelve crowns from the guild, taken against the house itself to pay for the great clock's bells. A guild copy pinned behind it was marked as not repaid, and nothing in her father's books showed any repayment. Unable to sleep after the clock stopped, Tamsin had gone down to look up the clock's contract, in case the guild asked who was responsible for keeping it. Beside it she found her father's final ledger, noticed two leaves that would not part, and cut the stitches with a penknife. She recalled that her father had drowned eleven winters earlier, and that her mother had died of fever four years before him. The guild's law book told her that at a Reckoning on Thaw Day any house with an unpaid guild debt was forfeit, with no appeal. She feared the guild would look hard at the house after the stopped clock, and she knew that Pim was asleep and Edwin Leckie was away. She folded the paper back and began reading the page again.
scenes.s3: By the end, Tamsin had decided to tell no one about the sewn page, not even Pim, and to deal with it alone and quickly, before anyone guessed there was anything to deal with. She and Pim went up from the river stairs together to make porridge, with Pim already planning the tools he would want for the clock. Before dawn, Tamsin had gone down the river stairs behind the clock-house to be alone and stood looking at the black gap of open water where the yards' drain kept the ice from closing. She could not swim and could not bear water above her knees, because at seven she had fallen into the millrace at Ambry while her father mended the mill clock, and had been hauled out by the hair by a miller's boy. She reminded herself that her father had died under the ice below Corran Weir, then put the thought away. Pim found her there and offered theories, that the steel pendulum rod had shrunk in the frost and the oil had thickened, and said he could fix it by noon if the guild would let him up the tower. Tamsin nearly confided in him but remembered that he could not keep a secret.
scenes.s4: By the end, Tamsin and Pim had been told by Corvin Slade, Warden of the Wharf, that the Reckoning would sit this year on Thaw Day, six weeks and more away, and Tamsin had left the Guildhall shaken by his hints about old accounts and by a veiled threat to Pim's future. Pim had been allowed to go up to the clock room and look at the clock, though not to touch it. A guild runner brought a summons to the house at ten, and Tamsin wore the Orrs' iron vault key on her belt as they crossed the bridge to meet Slade in the long room under the clock. Slade was a tall, thin, courteous man of about fifty-five with pale eyes and a silver-headed cane. He said the stopped clock was the house's shame and that every house must lay its books open at the Reckoning. He asked after Edwin Leckie, who was upriver in Hollin, and pointed out that the vault opened only to two keys, so without Leckie's key the house could not reach its own deeds. Tamsin insisted that the house's books were in order.
scenes.s5: By the end, Tamsin had broken her right wrist, the hand she wrote with, and a bargeman was taking her along Gilt Street to the bonesetter Hesketh Fane, with forty-four days left until Thaw Day. Two days after Lantern Night, with the great clock still stopped, Tamsin went to the guild vault with the Orrs' key and a copy of the sewn page, hoping to see the house's deeds. The vault clerk, a young man with a scrubbed pink face, explained that the vault opened only to two keys turned together, hers and Master Leckie's, and that the register said only that the deeds were held. She had hoped the deed would contradict the loan, and left with nothing. Walking back over the Chain Bridge, she went down the icy steps at the west end too fast, slipped on the third step and broke her wrist as she fell. A bargeman helped her up, and she kept him between herself and the clock-house window so Pim would not see her. At Fane's shop she began, to her own horror, to laugh.
scenes.s6: By the end, Tamsin's wrist was set and splinted, with a month in the splint ahead of her and no lifting until Thaw Day, and she had made up her mind to go north to Hollin herself to bring Edwin Leckie home. Hesketh Fane set the bone in the middle of the afternoon after giving her willow bark and poppy, and bound it with slats and linen into a sling. While she sat by his fire she told him everything: the sewn page, the four hundred and twelve crowns, Slade, the vault clerk and Leckie's absence. Fane agreed that Pim must not be told. He remembered her father worrying about money in the autumn of the bells, but doubted he had been ashamed, since he never owed anyone past the time. He asked where Leckie had gone, and she named his sister Bettany in Hollin. Fane spoke of Elsbet, a woman from the hills who had died three winters earlier, and of her empty blue pot for snowbells. Tamsin asked how long the ice road stayed open and promised to bring him a snowbell from Hollin, and Fane told her to bring herself back first.
scenes.s7: By the end, Tamsin left the guild pigeon loft with three homing pigeons in a wicker basket and the understanding that they could carry messages to the loft but nobody could send word back to her. Orla Finch, who kept the guild birds, had refused to ask where she was going or why. On the fourth morning after Lantern Night Tamsin climbed with difficulty to the loft above the west wharf, and Orla helped her up the ladder. Tamsin asked whether a person going north could send word home by bird. Orla explained that pigeons fly only by daylight and only home to their own loft, so messages could come to Callowmere but never go north. She showed Tamsin the tin tube and waxed thread for tying a message to the leg, and Tamsin tried writing with her left hand, producing shaky letters. Orla knew that Pim could not read and promised to read any message to him herself. She gave care instructions for the birds, refused any payment because Tamsin's father had once mended her clock for nothing, and asked only that her birds be brought back.
scenes.s8: By the end, Tamsin had hired Kit Ansel, a driver from Dunmere, and his dog sledge the Long Patience to take her north at dawn the next day, paying half the fare in advance, and she had told Pim only that she was going to fetch Master Leckie home for the Reckoning. Pim agreed to keep the house and wind the clocks, and he would hear her news through Orla's birds. Tamsin spent the afternoon of the seventh day at the ice-road stand, where the drivers refused her one after another because nobody would go beyond Dunmere in winter. Kit, a broad, amused man with a short brown beard, was going home to Dunmere anyway and agreed to go on to Hollin after haggling over the price. He named his six dogs: Hob, Fen, Bracken, Sloe, Rusk and little Tansy. Kit knew no Hollish, so Tamsin, whose mother had been a Hollin woman, would have to do the talking. Pim arrived, spotted a fault in Kit's sledge brake, and was told she was leaving. He read the time from their father's watch and handed it back to her.
scenes.s9: By the end, Tamsin and Kit were a day out of Callowmere on the ice road with a second sledge keeping pace behind them, and Tamsin was sure she was being followed by the man in the bottle-green coat she had noticed that morning. Kit had admitted that the other team belonged to Joss Merrow and that it stopped whenever they did. They left in the blue hour before sunrise, with the dogs in harness and the pigeon basket wedged at Tamsin's feet. Kit taught her commands such as hup, gee, haw and whoa, and she got Hob to turn right by shouting like someone owed money. They ran up the road marked by lantern stakes. At the north stairs Tamsin saw a lean man in a bottle-green coat with ink-stained cuffs counting coins into Joss Merrow's hand, and he watched her and her splint a moment too long. At midday, while the dogs were fed, she noticed a dark sledge far down the road that stopped when they stopped, and when they set off again it came on behind them.
scenes.s10: By the end, Tamsin lay awake in a room under the eaves of the inn at Ambry, doing sums that left her thirty-nine days to Thaw Day, listening to the mill race run under the ice and watching a lamp still burning in the Wheatsheaf across the green, where the man in the green coat was staying. Kit had told her that the clerk and Joss Merrow's dogs were there. After supper by the fire Kit asked what took a bookkeeper to Hollin in midwinter, and Tamsin gave him the story that Master Leckie, her father's partner and a sharer in the house, was wanted at the Reckoning and she was going to fetch him home. Kit accepted this without pressing, saying only that every fare had business they did not tell the driver. Tamsin kept her eyes away from the mill when they arrived and could not bear to think of the race where she had nearly drowned at seven. She paid for beds, stew and straw for the dogs left-handed, and hardly slept at all.
scenes.s11: By the end, the sledge carrying the guild clerk had been left far behind, but Tamsin knew he knew her name and her errand, and Kit, who distrusted him, had begun telling her about his dead brother. Leaving Ambry before sunrise, the Long Patience was overtaken by the other sledge, and the man in the bottle-green coat introduced himself as Dace Wilmot, clerk to the guild, travelling north on the Warden's business. He guessed she was going to fetch Master Leckie, asked where Leckie lodged and whether he had taken books or papers with him, and said he carried papers needing his signature. Tamsin told him nothing. Kit set the dogs running and left Joss Merrow's tired team behind. Kit said Wilmot asked questions like a horse-coper looking at teeth and that he paid the Warden wharf dues on every trip. Later he spoke of Dunmere and of his brother Davey, who went through the ice of Lake Dun five winters earlier. Tamsin did not mention her own father, but found she liked Kit and wanted to tell him.
scenes.s12: By the end, Tamsin and Kit were at Corran Weir at dusk, two days out of Callowmere, with the weir-keeper Brannock inviting her in for soup, one pigeon sent home with a note and two left in the basket. She had learned that the thaw bell in the tower beside the weir house would close the ice road by law whenever Brannock rang it, which might be a month before Thaw Day or after, and that nobody could say when. They had heard the weir long before they saw it, a great stone wall with water pouring over the crest and unsafe ice below. Brannock, a big slow old man, greeted Kit and asked nothing of her. He showed her the bell and its rope. At the bench in the yard Tamsin wrote a short note left-handed saying she was safe and on her way, which Kit helped her tie to a pigeon's leg before she let it go south. Looking down at the thin ice below the weir, she thought of her father drowning, and Brannock warned her never to trust ice there. The road behind them was empty.
scenes.s13: By the end, Tamsin had put a small brass wheel from her father's last load in her pocket beside his watch, and she and Kit had chosen to cross to the east side by an old track because the ice on the west side above the weir was rotten from a spring. That morning Brannock noticed her name and asked if she was Aldous Orr's daughter. He took her to the foot of the tower and showed her the place forty yards below the weir where her father had gone through the ice eleven years earlier. He told her that Aldous, coming south from Hollin with brass from the foundry, had refused the bank road in an early thaw and said he could beat the bell. The sledge had caught on the ice edge and Brannock saved most of the load, but the water took Aldous, and his body was not found until spring. Brannock had kept the brass wheel that rolled out of the canvas. Kit then reported the rotten ice, and the east track, with most of its stakes still standing, became their road.
scenes.s14: By the end, the ice on the old track had begun to split around Tamsin, who had gone wide toward the east bank with Kit calling to her to keep clear of a black crack that came running along the track behind her, while a second crack ran in from the left to meet it. Kit had taken the sledge up the bank road past the weir and out onto the upper ice, and had her walk behind it, knocking the ice with a long iron-shod ash pole to test it. The stakes along the old track leaned and some were missing, and the dogs went slowly with their ears flat, hearing the ice groan and tick. Tamsin counted her steps, trying to forget how deep the river was. Then the ice cracked like a pistol shot and a line opened at the grey stain where the spring entered, ran across the track behind her and came after her. She struck out toward the alders on the far bank, with the white ice beginning to spread apart.
scenes.s15: By the end, Kit had dragged Tamsin out of the river, soaked and half frozen, but little Tansy's foreleg had been hurt in the rescue, and Kit was walking Tamsin to a hut on the east bank where he promised a fire. The slab she stood on tipped and slid, and Tamsin went under the ice, remembering the millrace, with no idea which way was up. She surfaced in the hole and tried to climb out, but the edge kept breaking. Kit crawled out flat on his belly with the long spare line from the sledge and threw her a loop, and she got it round her shoulders. He shouted to Hob and the team to pull, and they dragged her out over the ice, she and Kit sliding along on their stomachs. During the pull the sledge slewed and Tansy at the back was caught between the ice and the sledge, and afterwards she would not put the leg down. Kit laid Tansy on the sledge beside the pigeon basket, and Tamsin, stiff and shivering, got to her feet.
scenes.s16: By the end, Tamsin was warm in a fisherman's hut on the east bank, her father's watch, the brass wheel and the pigeons all having survived the river, and she had told Kit Ansel everything about the debt, after which he swore to see her to Hollin and back again. Kit lit a fire, made her strip off her wet clothes and put on dry ones, and gave her hot broth. He brought Tansy in wrapped in his coat, her leg hurt but alive, and said a woman in Dunmere could treat it. The watch, though misted, was still ticking, and the wheel had come out of the river twice. Tamsin saw that his knuckles were raw from the rope and thought of Davey, who had had no one to throw him a rope. She told him about the clock stopping, the sewn page and the four hundred and twelve crowns, Slade, the Reckoning and Leckie's key. Kit was angry on her behalf, said he had no love for the guild, and promised to take her to Hollin and home. She said she could pay no more than agreed, and he said he had never asked.
scenes.s17: By the end, the sledge was running for the shore of Dunmere across the frozen lake, with Tansy riding in a nest of sacks and Kit about to take her to the dog-healer Hanne Roe. They had set out at first light the morning after the fishing hut. Tamsin was afraid of the ice, and Kit joked that a coach and four could dance on it. The river opened out into Lake Dun, where Kit stopped the team to take off his cap, as Dunmere folk did, because they said the lake remembered everyone it had kept. Tamsin pushed back her hood in turn, knowing his brother had gone through the ice there five years earlier. They followed a line of poles with red rags across the quiet white lake toward the town, and Tamsin checked her father's watch, which said it was not yet nine. Kit pointed out the Heron inn on the quay, and the narrow house with the crooked chimney and green shutters that had been his mother's, where he and Davey used to sit on the step. Hob smelled the dogs of the town and the team ran for the shore.
scenes.s18: By the end, Tansy was to stay in Dunmere with the dog-healer Hanne Roe and her daughter Mina, Kit would run only five dogs, and Tamsin had pawned her father's silver watch for a fortnight to pay for the binding and supplies, walking back to the yard with nothing but a pawn ticket in her coat. Hanne examined Tansy and said the bone was cracked and the cords torn, so the leg would knit but Tansy would never run in harness again. Kit had expected it. Mina, who wanted a dog of her own, was delighted when Hanne asked to keep her, and Kit agreed and said a quiet goodbye. Watching Hanne splint the leg, Tamsin thought of her own wrist, and Kit called them a matched pair. Hanne asked three crowns, and with the supplies the total was more than Tamsin's purse held. She refused Hanne's offer to wait. She sent a second pigeon with a note saying she was still safe, that Kit was good and that Pim should mind the house, leaving one bird in the basket. At the pawnbroker's she took a sum for the watch and a ticket good for a fortnight.
scenes.s19: By the end, Dace Wilmot was revealed to have been sitting on the next settle at the Heron all evening, close enough to hear everything Tamsin and Kit said about the debt, the vault keys and Slade, and he raised his cup to her with a polite smile. At the inn, they ate eel stew by the fire, and Tamsin laid the whole matter out for Kit: four hundred and twelve crowns borrowed from the guild against the house, with no sign it was ever repaid, and a vault that opened only to her key and Leckie's. She said her father always recorded the repayment of his debts, so he must have been hiding something or ashamed, and that Leckie would know. Kit guessed Leckie had run north from fear of somebody, and she named Slade, who wanted the house for its frontage on the wharf. Kit said Slade never left Callowmere in winter because of his knee and that the clerk had surely turned back at the weir. They planned to leave before dawn for the valley road and Hollin. Then she saw the pewter cup on the settle behind hers, and a sleeve with old ink stains.
scenes.s20: By the end, Tamsin and Kit had climbed the valley road at sunrise and sighted the smoke of the Hollin mine-heads far ahead. Tamsin still had not decided what to say to Edwin Leckie, and neither she nor Kit had spoken about Wilmot at the Heron. They crossed the end of Lake Dun before dawn, Tamsin thinking of Wilmot's cup lifted in the firelight and of Kit standing outside her door for a long time the night before. At the foot of the valley road he checked the dogs one by one, and Tamsin walked to spare them, her splint aching in the thin sharp cold. As the dogs began to labour on the steep pitches, Kit sang a made-up song full of verses about each dog, and the team found their stride. Tamsin tried a dozen ways of opening with Leckie, whom she had last seen in the autumn in the workshop turning his hat in his hands, looking as though he wanted to tell her something. She thought of her mother, a Hollin girl who had come down to the lake. At the top of the steepest pitch the sun came over the ridge, and Kit pointed out the mine smoke of Hollin.
scenes.s21: By the end, Tamsin and Kit have reached Hollin and stabled their five dogs at the Copper Kettle, but they have learned nothing about Edwin Leckie, and Tamsin has gone up alone to the well at the top of the town, where a small figure stands winding the handle with her back to the street. Hollin turns out to be a smoky mine town of grey stone whose people have shut every door and shutter against strangers. Tamsin knocks at a narrow house, where a woman bars the door on her; a man ducks into an alley, and a baker walks away at Leckie's name, so she just buys a roll and shares it with Kit. Her father's watch is still in a pawnbroker's drawer in Dunmere. Unnerved by the silence, she guesses that someone warned the town, and Kit points out that Dace Wilmot was behind them on the road, not ahead. At the inn the ostler takes Kit's coins and gives the dogs a warm stable, and Kit tends their feet. Tamsin reasons that everyone must come to the well sooner or later, and sets off up the hill alone, Kit promising to hear her if she shouts.
scenes.s22: By the end, Tamsin knows that Edwin Leckie is alive but ill with lung fever at his sister Bettany's house below the chapel, and that the town shut its doors because he asked it to, fearing men from the city. The old woman at the well, Isla Thorne, has told her to go at lamp-lighting, knock, and give her own name and her father's. Tamsin has promised to come afterwards and tell Isla how her mother Ysolde lived. Isla at first brushes Tamsin off in Hollish, saying she has no words for valley people, but Tamsin answers in the same tongue, learned from her mother, who was born in Hollin and married a Callowmere clockmaker. Isla recalls Ysolde as a girl who sang flat in chapel and once climbed a mine-head on a dare, and learns that she died of marsh fever when Tamsin was nine. Kit arrives with the dogs, understands none of it, and is told only that Leckie is alive; he thanks Isla in one of his two Hollish words, which makes her laugh. Isla then sets off down toward the chapel, and Kit follows carrying her pail.
scenes.s23: By the end, Tamsin has found Edwin Leckie alive but wasted and feverish in his sister Bettany's house, and he has told her he holds something that belongs to her, though a coughing fit stops him saying what. He has promised to tell her everything in the morning, swearing on her father's clock, and Bettany has told her and Kit to come back then by the chapel yard and knock twice. At dusk Tamsin knocks at the tall narrow house; Bettany, grey-haired and sharp, first denies that Leckie is there but opens when Tamsin gives Isla's name, her own, and her father Aldous Orr's. Inside, Leckie, sixty-one and looking eighty, mistakes the visitors for men sent by Slade and cries that he burned it. Recognising Tamsin, he weeps, speaks of her father coming north every winter for brass, asks after Pim, and says he was afraid and a coward. Asked whether Pim knows, Tamsin says not yet. Bettany ends the talk. As they leave, Leckie murmurs that the thing belongs to Tamsin and no one else must have it. A painted clock stands stopped in the corner.
scenes.s24: By the end, Tamsin knows her father repaid the 412-crown debt in gold to Corvin Slade, then guild treasurer, the week before he drowned, and that Leckie has a signed and sealed receipt hidden in Bettany's house along with the key; he refuses to tell anyone where until he can fetch it himself. Tamsin, hopeful for the first time, has written down everything he said with her left hand, and she and Kit have agreed they will get it; thirty-four days remain to Thaw Day, four of them the road home. In the morning Bettany goes out for more of Isla's draught, and Leckie, clearer, lets Kit stay because Tamsin trusts him. Tamsin tells him of the sewn page in her father's ledger. Leckie explains that Aldous borrowed the money for the great clock's bells, paid it back in gold, and gave Leckie the receipt to keep safe, which Leckie shoved in a drawer for eleven years. This autumn Slade summoned him, pressed him to sign the house away and hinted at the cold river; Leckie then understood what the paper was, and fled north with it and his key, falling ill on the road at Dunmere. Kit splits logs outside.
scenes.s25: By the end, Hollin is snowed in, Leckie is no stronger and still will not say where he put what he brought north, and Dace Wilmot, Slade's clerk, sits thawed and courteous in the taproom of the Copper Kettle, watching Tamsin and Kit. On the fourteenth day, with thirty-three days left to the Reckoning and four wanted for the run home, a great storm closes the road to the lake. That night a carter brings in Wilmot, half frozen, and Tamsin watches and does not help him. For six days the snow keeps falling, and Tamsin and Kit tunnel each morning to Bettany's house. On the twentieth night Wilmot sits at their table and offers fifty crowns for the old man's papers, payable in spring. Tamsin sees that the sum only works if the house is lost by then and refuses, and Wilmot remarks that people have accidents in snow. Kit seizes him and drags him toward the door; Tamsin holds Kit back, pointing out that a dead clerk would hang him and be laid at her door. Kit lets go, and Wilmot says he will remember her reasoning.
scenes.s26: By the end, Tamsin's splint is off and her thin, weak right wrist is in Isla's care, with a ball of beeswax to squeeze a hundred times morning and night until it can be crushed flat; Leckie is slowly mending, sitting up for an hour at a time, and says the hand will wind the great clock by Thaw Day, though he still puts off telling her about the thing he holds. The snow keeps falling and the road to the lake lies under twelve feet of white. Tamsin spends her days at Bettany's house reading aloud to Leckie while Kit, in the inn stable, mends every strap of the Long Patience's harness. Isla comes most afternoons to tend Leckie and sing Hollish songs, which bring back to Tamsin her mother's tunes and words. At night Tamsin lies awake worrying about Pim alone on Gilt Street. On the thirty-third day Isla unwinds the bandage put on by the bonesetter Hesketh Fane, praises his joinery, cuts off the splint thirty days after the fall, washes and salves the wasted wrist, and bends it painfully.
scenes.s27: By the end, Tamsin holds the proof she came for: the receipt is sewn into the lining of her coat, over her heart, and Leckie's brass key is buttoned in her coat pocket beside the Orrs' key on her belt. She also has a pressed snowbell that Isla gave her for Hesketh Fane, and a secret she has sworn in Hollish to keep: Isla told her privately that Leckie's heart is failing, that he will not see the summer, and that he must not be told. Kit, who suspects something, is put off with talk of hill business about the snow. On the thirty-eighth day Leckie stands unaided and has Kit walk him to Bettany's stopped painted clock, where he reaches behind the weights to a hidden ledge and takes out an oilskin packet. Inside are the key and a guild-sealed half-sheet, eleven winters old, reading paid in full, 412 crowns in gold, received of Aldous Orr, signed C. Slade. Tamsin weeps and laughs, and Kit whoops and lifts her off the floor. She unpicks a seam of her coat lining at the left breast and sews the receipt in with tight stitches. Leckie asks her to rehearse what she will say to Slade.
scenes.s28: By the end, Wilmot knows the hiding place in the clock was empty and that Tamsin carries what he wants. She has moved the brass key from her pocket to a hollow Kit cut in the heel of her left boot, pegged shut, while the receipt stays sewn in her coat lining. Sleepless by the stove, she resolves that Pim must be warned at first light, since any carter going down the valley could carry Wilmot's letter to Callowmere ahead of them. Two days earlier, when the road opened and the Kettle filled with carters, she and Kit had moved into Bettany's house, with the sledge loaded in the yard and the dogs in the woodshed. In the night Tamsin hears scraping at the shutters and wakes Kit, and they find Wilmot, unshaven and shabby, turned out of the inn when his silver ran out and sleeping in the smithy, kneeling at the painted clock with a long knife, prising at its back boards. Kit takes the blade on his leather sleeve, disarms him, carries him out and throws him into the drift, reminding him of his talk of accidents and warning him off the house. Kit's sleeve is cut but he is unhurt.
scenes.s29: By the end, Tamsin and Kit have left Hollin on the sledge, bound south toward the lake, and the last of Orla Finch's pigeons has flown home at first light with a note for Pim; the paper is in her coat and the key under her heel. In the dark before dawn they climb to the first bend of the lake road, Kit watching for Wilmot, who has not been seen since he was thrown out. The note, written the night before, says they are coming home, that the Warden's man knows their business, and that Pim must bar the shop at dark, open to no one he does not know, and keep his counsel. She releases the slate-blue hen at daylight. At Bettany's house Leckie, dressed and a little stronger, makes sure she has both paper and key, tells her to give Slade nothing, and says he will come down when the river opens; Tamsin keeps to herself what Isla told her about his heart. He and Kit part gently. Isla meets them on the road, blesses Tamsin in Hollish, tells her to keep her mouth shut until it is time, mocks Kit's fat dogs and thinness, and cackles at his clumsy thanks. Then the dogs pull them down the valley.
scenes.s30: By the end, Tamsin has lost her father's silver watch for good, since the Dunmere pawnbroker sold it to a drover, and she and Kit have set out across Lake Dun, having freed the sledge from a drift with Tamsin's weight on the harness and her right wrist holding. They reached Dunmere after dark and slept at the Heron. In the morning Tamsin counts her last money, enough to redeem the watch with interest, and Kit walks her along the quay and waits outside. The pawnbroker explains that the ticket allowed a fortnight, that he held the watch three days past because she seemed honest, and that he then sold it to a big man in a red muffler who gave no name and liked the lid. Tamsin thanks him and leaves the ticket on the counter. Kit asks nothing and offers no comfort, but buys her a mutton pie from a woman at a brazier and stands over her until she eats it. They harness up, her purse still holding enough for lodging and fish for the dogs, and at the lake's edge the sledge sticks nose first in a drift until Tamsin hauls on the harness beside Hob and it comes free onto the ice.
scenes.s31: By the end, the thaw bell has rung above Corran Weir and the ice road is closed by the Wardens' order and the old law, so old Brannock, the weir-keeper, sends Kit and Tamsin up the west bank road, to keep the river on their left and not go down to it. A warm south-west wind has put water on the ice and made it soft all morning, and the team reaches the weir a little before noon. Tamsin walks down to the grey crust of ice below the weir where her father went through eleven winters ago, hurrying home with brass for the clock-house, and remembers keeping a pot of soup hot for three hours at thirteen, Pim aged six, and a guild runner's knock on the third night. Kit joins her, asks how old she was, and says he still sees Davey's boots by the door after five years; she is grateful that he does not try to console her. The bell then rings and the river closes. Brannock comes out of the tower, moved to find her alive after hearing she had gone through the ice and been hauled out by Kit, and tells them the bank road will be a bog the whole way to the city.
scenes.s32: By the end, Tamsin, Kit, the five dogs and the sledge have crossed a flooded stretch of road at the edge of Ambry Fen by a rope Kit strung from a willow to a gatepost, and Tamsin, soaked and shaking, wearing Kit's coat over her own, walks south with him toward Callowmere. With the ice shut, they had scaled the steep, slushy bank and followed the old west-bank road through melting drifts and thorn tunnels in fine rain, Kit pausing every half mile to clear ice from the dogs' paws. In the afternoon the road drops to the fen, a wide sheet of standing water, and runs straight into a thirty-yard black stream with no way round; the river ice is closed and groaning. Kit insists they cross at once. He wades over with the rope, then takes the dogs, who swim, and the sledge, and Sloe goes under briefly. Tamsin, who cannot swim, ties the free end of the rope round her waist and crosses hand over hand with Kit beside her on the downstream side, her right wrist burning, and crawls out on the far bank. Kit cuts the rope free and they climb out of the fen with the dogs ahead.
scenes.s33: By the end, Tamsin and Kit are camped in a roofless shepherd's fold above Ambry Fen, a day's travel from Callowmere, with the paper still safe in her coat lining and the dogs bedded in a heap. They spent the day getting round the fen along drowned and slushy road, covering about nine miles. Tamsin gathers dead willow with the hatchet and finds her right wrist aches but holds. Kit dries everything by the fire, then tends each dog's feet in turn, Hob, Fen, Bracken, Sloe and Rusk, and when he reaches the small empty buckle, they both confess they keep counting six, for Tansy, left with Hanne Roe in Dunmere. Tamsin asks why the sledge is called the Long Patience, and Kit explains that his mother used to say the lake has a long patience and only needs you to be in a hurry once; she stood on the quay each morning that spring until the ice went out, after Davey. Kit says he now reads the name each morning so that he is never the one in a hurry. They talk about after Thaw Day: Tamsin will sleep a week, pay her bills and hear the clock strike; Kit will wait in Callowmere until the river opens and then go home.
scenes.s34: By the end, Tamsin has been stopped and searched at the north gate of Callowmere by four guild men acting on the Warden's orders, and they found nothing: the receipt sewn in her coat lining and the key in her boot heel went unnoticed, and the folded paper with the pressed snowbell stayed put when one of them shook her mother's hymn book. They found only a hairbrush, a shift, a pencil, a purse with four pennies and a stale oatcake, and Tamsin told them to tell the Warden she was home. Earlier that day she and Kit left the fold before light, found the fen frozen hard and the road easier, and passed farm folk, one of whom gave them buttermilk. From the gibbet hill she saw Callowmere's smoke on the horizon. Beside the road the river ice, with the old ice-road stakes still standing, lay smooth and shut, and Kit proposed using it to save an hour; Tamsin refused because the bell had rung, and Kit, remembering the name on his sledge, gave in. She wished she could tell Pim she was almost home, having no bird left and no watch.
scenes.s35: By the end, Tamsin is home in the clock-house on Gilt Street, has told Pim everything about the debt, Leckie and the receipt except Leckie's failing heart, and has let him feel the paper sewn in her coat; she has made him promise to wait two days and lay it before the guild on Thaw Day rather than shout it in the street. Pim is hurt that she did not tell him before she left, but lets her take his hand, and says he wants to climb the great clock's tower the next day. Pim runs out to greet her and Kit, who beds the dogs in the coal shed and sleeps on the workshop bench. Pim reports what happened while she was away: the workshop stove smoked, Master Garrow took away the half-finished tower clock, the coal merchant refuses credit, a stone went through the shop window, and guild men searched the house, listing and chalking every tool and clock, including their father's bench, which Pim washed and which was chalked again after the guild's letter came. Orla Finch read him the letter, summoning the house of Orr & Leckie to the Reckoning on Thaw Day on pain of forfeit. Pim had told everyone it was a mistake and now sees it is not.
scenes.s36: By the end, Pim has found why the great clock stopped on Lantern Night: a pin in the pallet arbor of the escapement has sheared, every gear is sound, and he promises to make a new pin that night on the lathe and fit it in the morning. Tamsin, meanwhile, has learned what is being said on the wharf: that the Warden means to seize the house on Thaw Day before the whole guild and has a man ready to install, though Wilmot, his green-coated clerk, has not been seen since he went north. Earlier that morning Tamsin and Pim climbed the outside stairs to the guild loft above the wharf, where Orla Finch shows her that all three pigeons came home safely, from Corran, Dunmere and the Hollin road, each with its note delivered by Orla to Pim, who had forgotten to mention it. Tamsin holds the small grey hen. Orla tells her to come back and report how it goes, but not before, as she has no patience for hope. After dinner Pim goes across to the Guildhall tower with tools and caraway biscuits for the porter, while Tamsin spends the afternoon over the house's books in the counting room, listening to every clock in the house tick and glancing out toward the stopped tower clock across the river.
scenes.s37: By the end, Tamsin and Pim have been admitted by the porters to the Guildhall on Thaw Day for the Reckoning, summoned as Orr & Leckie, clockmakers of Gilt Street; the key is hidden in the heel of her left boot, the receipt in her coat lining and the Orrs' key at her belt, and Pim carries the new pin he made in the night. Kit has gone ahead to hold a place near the front of the hall. They leave the clock-house in the morning thaw, Pim in their father's too-small grey coat, and the town streams toward the Guildhall to see the house fall. Tamsin hears bystanders say her father ran up the debt and hushes Pim, who talks to everyone; he swears he has told nobody, not even the baker's cat. The great clock has stood at seven minutes to midnight for forty-six days. On the Chain Bridge, where she fell, her right wrist holds as she grips the chain, and Pim steadies her on the icy step. The river below is breaking up and the ice-road stand is deserted. The Guildhall square is packed, and the porters let her pass.
scenes.s38: By the end, Tamsin has opened the guild vault with both keys, laid the receipt beside the treasurer's book, and heard Dace Wilmot testify that Slade boasted of receiving Aldous Orr's gold; Slade's cane has clattered to the floor and the hall is in uproar. At the Reckoning at noon, the Warden Corvin Slade reads out the 412-crown debt against Orr & Leckie, and Tamsin says it was paid in gold eleven years ago into the treasurer's hand and asks for the vault to be opened. Slade points out that it needs two keys and that Leckie has one; she says it is not in Hollin. Master Haverill leads them down. Tamsin sets the Orrs' key in one lock, prises open the heel of her boot with Pim's penknife, takes out Leckie's key and turns both. The treasurer's book of that year shows the loan and no repayment, signed C. Slade, Treasurer. She unpicks her coat lining and lays the receipt beside it, and Haverill reads it aloud. Slade calls it a copied or stolen paper from a runaway. Wilmot, thin and shabby in his green coat, comes forward: Slade left him penniless in Hollin, and three winters ago at a supper told him the clockmaker had brought him the money and the river had saved him from entering it.
scenes.s39: By the end, the guild has struck the Orr & Leckie debt from its books as paid and ordered the Warden's accounts opened within the week, with Slade keeping none of them meanwhile; Slade has left the hall alone, and Pim has fitted the new pin so that the great clock of Callowmere runs again, striking four, while Tamsin watches from the landing. Master Haverill puts the question to the guild, and the ayes come; the under-clerk rules a line through the entry in the great book. A second vote opens the Warden's books. Slade does not argue, stoops to retrieve his cane himself, says the guild may do as it pleases, and walks the length of the room, tap and drag, while nobody looks at him. Tamsin thinks of her father, then puts the thought away. Pim asks leave to go up, and Haverill says the guild has waited forty-six days for someone to ask. By Haverill's watch it is twenty minutes to four; Kit stands at the foot of the tower shouting the minutes. In the clock chamber Pim removes the sheared pin, fits the new one, winds, sets the hands, and at four starts the strike and the pendulum. The square roars, and Pim calls to Tamsin to listen.
scenes.s40: By the end, Tamsin has promised to visit Kit at Dunmere in the summer and has given Hesketh Fane the pressed snowbell from Hollin, which he has put in a box on his shelf; she stands at her door as the great clock strikes noon. On the morning after Thaw Day the river breaks up. Sitting on the river stairs eating chestnuts, Kit says he will stay in Callowmere until the river and the bank road are open, three or four weeks, keeping the bench in Pim's workshop, and then go home to Tansy and the other dogs. He asks her to come and see the lake in summer and keep his accounts from the jetty; she says she will never go in the water above the knee, but agrees. They visit Fane's shop. He says he wept at hearing the clock strike four the day before, examines her wrist, pronounces it a clean knit, and learns that Isla cut the splint and set her squeezing beeswax. Tamsin gives him the snowbell, as she promised, and he remembers his late wife Elsbet telling of the slopes above Hollin; they had always put off going, and it has been three winters. Fane teases Kit about returning to his lake. They walk home up Gilt Street.

chapters.1: By the end, Tamsin Orr was alone with the knowledge that her late father had borrowed four hundred and twelve crowns from the guild against the house, with no sign it was ever repaid, and the Warden of the Wharf had told her the Reckoning would sit on Thaw Day, six weeks and more away. She had decided to tell no one, not even Pim, and to act alone. On Lantern Night the great Guildhall clock that her father and Edwin Leckie built stopped at seven minutes to midnight in front of the city, and the crowd turned to look at the Orrs (scene 1). That night Tamsin, unable to sleep, found a page sewn shut in her father's last ledger, which recorded the guild loan and a guild copy marked not repaid, and she read the guild's law on forfeiture at a Reckoning (scene 2). At dawn on the river stairs she recalled nearly drowning in the Ambry millrace and resolved not to confide in Pim, who could not keep a secret (scene 3). Warden Corvin Slade then summoned the house, announced the Reckoning, hinted at old accounts, noted that the vault needed Leckie's key as well as hers, and let Pim look at the clock but not touch it (scene 4).
chapters.2: By the end, Tamsin had a splinted right wrist, three homing pigeons, and a sledge driver booked to take her north at dawn to fetch Edwin Leckie from Hollin, and she had told Pim only that she was going to bring Leckie home for the Reckoning. At the guild vault the clerk would not show the deeds without both keys, and on her way home she fell on the icy bridge steps and broke her wrist (scene 1). At the bonesetter Hesketh Fane's shop her wrist was set, and she confided the sewn page and the debt to him; he doubted her father had been ashamed, and she resolved to go north to Hollin (scene 2). Orla Finch gave her three pigeons at the guild loft and explained that they could fly only home and only by day, so word could go south but not come north (scene 3). At the ice-road stand drivers refused her until Kit Ansel agreed to take her, and she told Pim her cover story, leaving him to keep the house (scene 4).
chapters.3: By the end, Tamsin and Kit had reached Corran Weir at dusk, two days out, and Tamsin knew that the thaw bell there could close the ice road at any moment, perhaps before Thaw Day. She had sent the first of her pigeons home with a note, and they were being followed. On leaving Callowmere, Kit taught her the dog commands, and she spotted the man in the green coat paying Joss Merrow at the north stairs, whose sledge then trailed them all day (scene 1). At the Ambry inn, beside the mill where she had nearly drowned, Kit asked her errand and she gave only the story of fetching Leckie; she lay awake listening to the water (scene 2). Next morning the man introduced himself as Dace Wilmot, clerk to the guild, and probed her about Leckie and what he took with him until Kit outran him; Kit then spoke of his drowned brother Davey (scene 3). At Corran Weir the keeper Brannock showed her the bell, she wrote home by pigeon, and she looked at the dangerous ice below the weir (scene 4).
chapters.4: By the end, Tamsin was warm and safe in a fisherman's hut on the east bank after falling through the ice, having told Kit Ansel the whole story of the debt, and Kit had sworn to see her to Hollin and back. The dog Tansy had been badly hurt in the rescue. At Corran, Brannock recognised her as Aldous Orr's daughter, showed her where he drowned below the weir, and gave her a brass wheel from her father's load; Kit chose the old east track because the west ice was rotten (scene 1). On that track, as Tamsin walked behind the sledge testing the ice with a pole, a crack opened behind her and ran after her (scene 2). The ice gave way and she went under, but Kit crawled out and looped a rope round her and the dogs hauled her out; Tansy's foreleg was injured by the sledge (scene 3). In the hut Kit lit a fire, tended Tansy, and heard the story of the loan, the Reckoning and Slade, and promised to take her to Hollin and home again (scene 4).
chapters.5: By the end, Tamsin and Kit were on the valley road to Hollin with the mine smoke in sight, but Tamsin had pawned her father's watch, Tansy had been left behind in Dunmere, one pigeon remained, and Dace Wilmot had overheard everything she told Kit. They crossed Lake Dun at first light with Tansy riding in a nest of sacks; Kit took off his cap on the lake in memory of his brother, and they reached Dunmere (scene 1). At Hanne Roe's yard the healer said Tansy would never run in harness again and would stay with Hanne and her daughter Mina, so Kit had five dogs; Tamsin, short of money, sent a second pigeon home and pawned the watch for a fortnight (scene 2). At the Heron that night Tamsin laid out the debt, the keys and Slade for Kit, and then discovered Wilmot on the next settle, who raised his cup to her (scene 3). Leaving before dawn, they climbed the valley road, with Kit singing to the dogs and Tamsin worrying what to say to Leckie, until they saw the smoke of Hollin (scene 4).
chapters.6: By the end of the chapter, Tamsin knows that Edwin Leckie is alive in Hollin and that her father paid the 412-crown guild debt in gold to Corvin Slade the week before he drowned. Leckie holds a signed receipt and a key, hidden somewhere in his sister Bettany's house, and refuses to say where until he can fetch them himself. Tamsin, newly hopeful, has written down his account; thirty-four days remain to Thaw Day, four of them the road home. She and Kit arrive in the mountain town to find every door shut against them (scene 1). At the well, the old healer Isla Thorne, who knew Tamsin's mother Ysolde, is answered in Hollish and explains that Leckie asked the town to shut out strangers; she tells Tamsin to call at lamp-lighting and extracts a promise to tell her of Ysolde's life (scene 2). At Bettany's house Tamsin finds Leckie feverish and frightened, saying he holds something of hers but is too ill to say more (scene 3). Next morning, with Kit present, he tells of the receipt, Slade's threats and why he fled (scene 4).
chapters.7: By the end of the chapter, Tamsin has the receipt sewn into her coat lining and the key hidden in the heel of her left boot, and Dace Wilmot knows she has them after his night search of Bettany's clock found nothing; she resolves to warn Pim at first light. She also carries Isla's pressed snowbell for Hesketh Fane and a sworn secret that Leckie's heart is failing. Heavy snow shuts Hollin, and Wilmot, rescued half frozen, offers fifty crowns for Leckie's papers, which Tamsin refuses; Kit nearly throws him into the snow before she restrains him (scene 1). Isla cuts off Tamsin's splint, gives her a ball of beeswax to rebuild her wrist, and sings the Hollish songs back to her while Leckie slowly mends (scene 2). On the thirty-eighth day Leckie retrieves the packet from the painted clock, and Tamsin sews the receipt into her coat; Isla then tells her about his heart (scene 3). That night Wilmot breaks in and prises at the empty clock, Kit throws him out, and the key goes into Tamsin's boot (scene 4).
chapters.8: By the end of the chapter, Tamsin and Kit have crossed a flooded stretch of road at Ambry Fen by rope and are walking south toward Callowmere with the dogs; the thaw bell has closed the ice road behind them, so they must use the bank road, and Tamsin's father's watch is gone for good. Before leaving Hollin she sent the last pigeon home with a warning for Pim, promised to keep Leckie a place by the stove, and received Isla's blessing for the road (scene 1). At Dunmere the pawnbroker had sold the watch to a drover; Kit silently bought her a pie, and she helped free the sledge from a drift on the lake shore (scene 2). At Corran Weir she faced the place where her father drowned eleven years before, told Kit about it, heard the thaw bell ring, and met the weir-keeper Brannock, who sent them to the bank road (scene 3). At Ambry Fen a flooded stream cut the road, and Kit took the dogs, the sledge and Tamsin across on a rope, though she cannot swim (scene 4).
chapters.9: By the end of the chapter, Tamsin is home on Gilt Street with Pim, who knows the whole story except Leckie's heart, and the pair have learned both what the guild plans and what is wrong with the great clock: a sheared pin in the escapement, which Pim will replace. Orla Finch reports gossip that the Warden means to take the house on Thaw Day, and that Wilmot has not returned (scene 4). Earlier, camped at a shepherd's fold above Ambry Fen, Kit tended the dogs, admitted he keeps counting six after leaving Tansy behind, explained the name Long Patience, and asked what Tamsin will do after Thaw Day (scene 1). Next day, near Callowmere, Kit was tempted by the shut river ice and gave in when she refused; at the north gate the Warden's men searched her and found neither the receipt nor the key (scene 2). At the clock-house Pim told her of the chalk, the guild's letter and the lost tower clock; she told him everything and he promised to wait for Thaw Day (scene 3). At the guild loft Orla showed her all three pigeons home, and Pim found the pin (scene 4).
chapters.10: By the end of the chapter, the guild has struck the Orr & Leckie debt from its books as paid, ordered the Warden's accounts opened within the week, and watched Slade walk out alone; Pim has fixed the great clock, which strikes again, and Tamsin has promised to visit Kit at Dunmere in summer, with Kit staying in Callowmere until the river opens. On Thaw Day Tamsin, Pim and Kit, who holds a place at the rail, go through muttering crowds and across the Chain Bridge to the Guildhall, the key in Tamsin's boot and the receipt in her coat (scene 1). At the Reckoning Slade reads out the debt, Tamsin opens the vault with the two keys, the treasurer's book shows no repayment, and she lays the receipt beside it; Slade dismisses it, but Wilmot testifies that Slade boasted of taking Aldous's gold (scene 2). The vote follows, the debt is struck and Slade leaves; Pim fits his new pin and restarts the great clock at four (scene 3). The next morning Tamsin and Kit sit on the river stairs and she accepts his summer invitation; she gives Hesketh Fane the snowbell, and the clock strikes noon (scene 4).
